raw_response:
I am 57 this year, and I have worked these 6 mu for many years, so I mostly do what is steady. Our place usually does wheat and then maize, one after the other, and I will keep that. I do not want to take big risks. If wheat is weak, the whole year feels tight, and if maize misses the planting window after wheat harvest, yield drops fast. I watch what the neighbors do and follow the local timing.

For wheat, I will sow in early October like usual, not too early and not too late. I will use a common improved seed from the local dealer, not the most expensive one. Fertilizer, I will still use, because if I save too much on that, the wheat ears get small. But I also cannot spend carelessly. So I will put a base fertilizer before sowing, then one topdressing around jointing if the wheat looks all right. With irrigation from the well, I plan about three times for wheat: once after sowing if the soil is dry, once around overwintering or turning green, and once at jointing or heading depending on rain. If weeds or aphids show up, I will spray; if not serious, I will not add extra medicine.

For maize, I will plant right after wheat harvest in June. That time is always rushed, so I will keep tillage simple and get the seed in quickly. I will use hybrid maize seed because local farmers all use that and yield is better. I will apply fertilizer, but not too much at once. Usually some goes at planting, then I add more at the big bell mouth stage. Maize depends on summer rain, so if rain is normal maybe one irrigation is enough, and if it turns dry I will give one more. I do not like spending too much on pumping water, but if the crop curls from drought, that loss is bigger. My wife and I do most of the work ourselves, and if harvest gets tight maybe I hire a little machine service, but not much labor by hand.
